summary: NASA Locator ranks 36 Earth sites by how closely they resemble permanent Moon base sites and Mars targets across 11 parameters, such as relief, temperature, precipitation, wind, ice and caves. Every value is traced to a source, and missing data is shown instead of treated as zero. Users can also test their own location using NASA POWER climate data.
details:
NASA Locator helps engineers and scientists choose where on Earth to test equipment, procedures and science for permanent Moon base sites (Shackleton rim, a pit in Mare Tranquillitatis) and Mars (Jezero). It ranks 36 Earth sites by similarity to the selected target.

How it works: for each of 11 parameters (rock origin, relief, four temperature measures, precipitation, wind, ice or permafrost, caves or lava tubes, interest for life detection), the site's value is compared with the target. Similarity = 1 / (1 + (difference / tolerance)^2), so a difference equal to the tolerance gives 50%. The scores are combined as a weighted average (weights 0-5). Users can change weights or pick one of 7 task profiles, and the ranking updates instantly in the browser.

Honesty about data: every value has an origin label (measured, from literature, or inferred) and a source link: 317 values, 42 sources. Empty values are not counted as zero. A "Data, %" indicator shows how many parameters could be compared, and below 50% the result is marked as approximate.

Pages: Locator (ranking and globe), Comparison (two places side by side), My Site (enter coordinates, fill climate from NASA POWER, compare your own site) and Methodology (formula, tolerances, sources, and what Earth cannot reproduce: gravity and radiation).

Tools: Python, Django, SQLite, JavaScript. The same algorithm was implemented in Python and JavaScript and gave identical results on 1982 test cases.

Limitations: tolerances were chosen by the authors and are not yet calibrated with planetary scientists; climate comes from a grid cell of about 50 km; the list of 36 sites is a manual selection.

Use of AI: an AI assistant (Claude) was used to help write and review code and documentation. The site list, parameters, tolerances and sources were selected and checked by the team. Calculations are deterministic and do not use AI at runtime.

Source code: https://github.com/David-99-it/earth-analogs-202
